title: Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) Cipher Suites for Transport Layer Security (TLS)
summary: Describes key exchange algorithms for TLS based on Elliptic Curve Cryptography, specifically ECDH key agreement in a handshake and ECDSA as an authentication mechanism. It is informational. It was replaced by RFC 8422.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4492 adds elliptic curve cryptography to TLS. It defines new ways for a client and server to agree on a shared secret, new ways for the client to prove who it is, and two extensions that let them agree on which curves to use. The point is to keep the same security with smaller keys, which matters on small devices.

what does the supported elliptic curves extension do
subtitle: Adding elliptic curve key exchange and signatures to TLS.

tldr.problem: TLS was built around RSA and Diffie-Hellman, which need large keys. On small devices such as mobile phones, large keys cost power, memory, bandwidth and computation, and elliptic curve cryptography gives the same security with much smaller keys.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4492 defines five key exchange algorithms that use Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman, with either long-term or ephemeral keys and either ECDSA or RSA signatures, plus three client authentication mechanisms. It also defines two TLS extensions so that a client and server can agree on which curves and point formats to use.
tldr.outcome: The document also defines 25 new cipher suites and marks four of them as the ones servers should support and clients should support at least one of. It is an Informational document that was later obsoleted by RFC 8422 and updated by RFC 5246, RFC 7027 and RFC 7919.

today: RFC 4492 is an Informational document that has been obsoleted by RFC 8422, and updated by RFC 5246, RFC 7027 and RFC 7919.

sections.title: Why Elliptic Curves in TLS
sections.content:
Elliptic Curve Cryptography is a public-key system that offers equivalent security with smaller key sizes than prevalent systems such as RSA. The RFC gives a table of approximate comparable key sizes for symmetric-key, elliptic curve and DH, DSA and RSA systems, based on the best-known algorithms for attacking them. A 128-bit symmetric key corresponds to a 283-bit ECC key or a 3072-bit RSA key.

Smaller keys mean savings in power, memory, bandwidth and computational cost, which is what makes ECC attractive in constrained environments such as mobile and wireless devices.

The document describes additions to TLS that apply to both TLS version 1.0 and TLS version 1.1. In particular it defines the use of Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman key agreement with long-term or ephemeral keys to establish the TLS premaster secret, and the use of fixed ECDH certificates and ECDSA to authenticate the peers. How the master secret is derived from the premaster secret, and how the bulk encryption and MAC keys and initialisation vectors are then generated, is independent of the key exchange algorithm and is not affected by ECC.
sections.plainLanguage: A 128-bit symmetric key has the same strength as a 283-bit ECC key, but an RSA key would need 3072 bits. Smaller keys save power, memory and bandwidth, which matters most on phones and other small devices.

sections.title: The Five Key Exchange Algorithms
sections.content:
The RFC introduces five ECC-based key exchange algorithms for TLS. All of them use ECDH to compute the premaster secret, and they differ only in the lifetime of the ECDH keys, long-term or ephemeral, and in the mechanism, if any, used to authenticate them. They mirror the existing DH_DSS, DHE_DSS, DH_RSA, DHE_RSA and DH_anon algorithms.

In ECDH_ECDSA, the server certificate must contain an ECDH-capable public key and be signed with ECDSA. No ServerKeyExchange message is sent, because the certificate already holds everything the client needs. The client makes an ECDH key pair on the same curve as the server's long-term public key and sends its public key in the ClientKeyExchange message, and both sides run the ECDH operation to get the shared secret.

In ECDHE_ECDSA, the server certificate holds an ECDSA-capable key and is signed with ECDSA. The server sends an ephemeral ECDH public key and the curve it belongs in the ServerKeyExchange message, and signs both with ECDSA. The client generates its own ECDH key pair on that curve and sends its public key. This algorithm, and ECDHE_RSA, provide forward secrecy.

ECDH_RSA works like ECDH_ECDSA except that the server certificate is signed with RSA, and ECDHE_RSA works like ECDHE_ECDSA except that the server certificate holds an RSA public key authorised for signing and the ServerKeyExchange signature is made with the matching RSA private key.

ECDH_anon sends no certificates at all. The server sends an ephemeral ECDH public key and the curve, but does not sign them. Because nothing is authenticated, this algorithm is open to man-in-the-middle attacks, and implementations should provide authentication by other means.

The RFC notes that there is no structural difference between an ECDH key and an ECDSA key. A certificate issuer may use the X.509 v3 keyUsage and extendedKeyUsage extensions to restrict what an ECC public key may be used for, and the RFC calls a key ECDH-capable when its use in ECDH is permitted.
sections.plainLanguage: The five algorithms all use the same shared-secret calculation. They differ in two ways: whether the keys are long-lived or made fresh for each connection, and whether the server signs the handshake with an ECDSA or an RSA key. Fresh keys give forward secrecy, meaning a later theft of the server's private key does not expose earlier sessions.

sections.title: Client Authentication
sections.content:
The RFC defines three client authentication mechanisms, each named after the type of client certificate involved: ECDSA_sign, ECDSA_fixed_ECDH and RSA_fixed_ECDH.

ECDSA_sign works with any of the non-anonymous ECC key exchange algorithms, and also with the non-ECC key exchange algorithms defined in TLS itself. The client must hold a certificate containing an ECDSA-capable public key signed with ECDSA, and proves possession of the private key by including a signature in the CertificateVerify message.

ECDSA_fixed_ECDH and RSA_fixed_ECDH are usable with ECDH_ECDSA and ECDH_RSA only. Their use with ECDHE_ECDSA and ECDHE_RSA is prohibited, because a long-term ECDH client key would spoil the forward secrecy of those algorithms. The client must hold a certificate containing an ECDH-capable public key signed with ECDSA, or with RSA for the second mechanism, and the client's ECDH key must be on the same curve as the server's certified ECDH key, which may limit the mechanism to closed environments. The client sends an empty ClientKeyExchange and no CertificateVerify message, because the client's public key is already in its certificate and reaching the same premaster secret on both sides proves possession of the private key.

The server asks for ECC-based client authentication by naming the certificate types it wants in its CertificateRequest message, and must not name any type that is prohibited for the negotiated key exchange. If the client has no suitable certificate or does not want to use one, it sends a client Certificate message with no certificates, and the CertificateVerify message is not sent.
sections.plainLanguage: When a server asks the client to prove who it is, it names the certificate types it will accept. The client sends a matching certificate, and one of three mechanisms is used to show it holds the private key that goes with it.

sections.title: Extensions for Curves and Point Formats
sections.content:
Two TLS extensions are defined here. The Supported Elliptic Curves Extension and the Supported Point Formats Extension let the two ends negotiate which curves and which point formats to use, where a point format says how a public key point is written on the wire, such as compressed or uncompressed.

The client enumerates the curves it supports and the point formats it can parse in its ClientHello message. The server enumerates the point formats it can parse in its ServerHello message. These extensions matter most for constrained clients, which may support only a few curves or point formats.

A client that proposes ECC cipher suites should include the extensions. Servers implementing ECC cipher suites must support them, and when a client uses them the server must not negotiate an ECC cipher suite unless it can complete the handshake while respecting the client's chosen curves and compression techniques. That removes the possibility of a handshake that is agreed and then aborted because the client cannot handle the server's key.

The client must not include the extensions if it proposes no ECC cipher suites at all. A client that does propose ECC cipher suites may leave them out, in which case the server is free to choose any of the curves or point formats it has defined. In a session resumption the server simply ignores both extensions, because they only matter when a new session is negotiated.

The curves are named by numbers in the extension, covering the SEC 2 named curves from sect163k1 at value 1 through secp521r1 at value 25, with a reserved range for private use and two values that signal support for arbitrary prime or characteristic-2 curves.
sections.plainLanguage: The two ends may not support the same curves. These extensions let the client list the curves it can handle, in order of preference, and the server list the point formats it can read. A server that receives the list must stay within it.

sections.title: Cipher Suites
sections.content:
The RFC defines 25 new cipher suites that use the key exchange algorithms of Section 2. Each name carries its own meaning: the key exchange algorithm, then the bulk cipher, then the hash algorithm. Five groups of five suites are defined, one group for each key exchange algorithm, and each group offers NULL, RC4 128, 3DES in CBC mode, AES 128 in CBC mode and AES 256 in CBC mode, all with SHA.

Server implementations should support all four of TLS_ECDH_ECDSA_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA, TLS_ECDH_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA, TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA and TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA. Client implementations should support at least one of them.
sections.plainLanguage: Each new cipher suite pairs one of the five key exchange algorithms with a bulk cipher and a hash algorithm. Servers should offer four specific suites, and clients need at least one of those four.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of the TLS specification apply to ECC handshakes as well, and the RFC points to the ECC literature for the parts specific to elliptic curves.

The first issue is curve selection. Beyond size, the structure of the curve matters. As a general principle it is more conservative to use curves with as little algebraic structure as possible, so random curves are more conservative than special curves such as Koblitz curves, and curves over a field with a random prime are more conservative than curves over a field whose prime has a special form. The RFC also notes that algebraic structure can lead to implementation efficiencies, so conservatism has to be balanced against efficiency. Concrete attacks are known against only very few special classes of curves, such as supersingular curves, and those classes are excluded from the ECC standards the RFC references.

The second issue is that a single curve used everywhere is a single point of failure. An attack on that curve could compromise a large number of keys, so this concern may also need to be balanced against the efficiency and interoperability gains of widely used curves.

The third issue is forward secrecy, which means session keys are not compromised if the static, certified keys of the server and client are compromised. ECDHE_ECDSA and ECDHE_RSA give that protection if the server's key is later stolen, while ECDH_ECDSA and ECDH_RSA do not. If the client is using a static, certified key, ECDSA_sign client authentication gives the same protection against later client key compromise, while ECDSA_fixed_ECDH and RSA_fixed_ECDH do not. So complete forward secrecy needs ECDHE_ECDSA or ECDHE_RSA for key exchange, with ECDSA_sign for client authentication if the client is authenticated.
sections.plainLanguage: Three things matter. First, not all curves are equally safe, and the safer ones have less special structure. Second, if everyone uses the same curve, breaking it would break many keys at once. Third, only the ephemeral key exchanges keep past sessions safe if a server's private key is later stolen.
